processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas, partly oxidised, rolled and finished with a charcoal or electric roast; no method peculiar to this tea is recorded.
harvest_season: Typical of Wuyi rock teas, a single spring picking; no cultivar-specific timing is recorded.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark strips, as is usual for roasted Wuyi oolong.
appearance_liquor: Orange to amber, typical of a medium-roast rock tea.
appearance_wet: As with other rock teas, broad leaves with darkened edges.
taste_profile: Few reliable tasting notes exist; expect the roast and mineral grip common to Wuyi rock teas, and judge the aroma for yourself.

brewing.notes: Standard rock-tea brewing: near-boiling water and short steeps in a small vessel.

vintage_note: Sold like other Wuyi rock teas: by the year of the spring harvest, usually after the roast has rested. Small named varieties like this come in small lots, so ask for year and growing area.
description:
Bai Rui Xiang is one of the many named varieties of Wuyi rock tea, listed alongside far better-known names such as Rou Gui and Shui Xian. The name reads as white auspicious fragrance, and beyond that it remains a tea with little written about it.

Nothing about its making is recorded as unusual, so assume the Wuyi pattern: partial oxidation, rolling and a roast that shapes much of the final character.

Brew it like its neighbours, hot and quick, and pay attention from one steep to the next. A fair description of its aroma has yet to be settled in print, which makes your own notes as useful as anyone's.

When buying, treat the name as a starting point and ask the seller about year, roast and place.
history: Little is documented about Bai Rui Xiang beyond its place in lists of named Wuyi varieties. Who selected it, and when, is not established.
